planting.note: Direct-sow in fall so seed overwinters and stratifies naturally, or moist-cold stratify seed 30 days before an early-spring sowing.

directions: Sow seed shallowly in fall or cold-stratify before a spring sowing, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the plant forms a basal rosette its first year and sends up a tall flowering stalk the following season before setting seed. Field thistle is one of the least aggressive native thistles, staying put in a clump rather than spreading like weedy introduced thistles, and its large pink-purple blooms are a magnet for bumblebees, swallowtails, fritillaries, and migrating hummingbirds. Leave the finished flower heads standing into fall so goldfinches can strip the down and seed. Give it room at the back of a meadow planting since the silvery, spine-edged foliage and flower stalks get tall by late summer.

planting.note: Sow in fall into consistently moist soil so seed stratifies over winter; keep beds evenly damp through spring germination.

directions: Plant in consistently wet to moist soil in a low spot, rain garden, or pond margin with full to partial sun; unlike its spinier upland relatives, swamp thistle has a nearly spineless stem that is comfortable to handle. It grows as a rosette the first year and flowers the second or third year on tall stalks topped with clusters of pink-purple blooms that are a favorite nectar stop for swallowtails, bumblebees, and the American goldfinch, which later feeds on the down-tufted seed. Because it needs sustained moisture, it is best suited to wet meadows and streambank plantings rather than average garden beds.

planting.note: Direct-sow after the soil warms in spring into lean, well-drained soil; seed needs light contact, so press in rather than bury.

directions: Sow into poor, dry, sunny soil where richer conditions would cause it to flop, and thin seedlings to give each plant room to branch. Curlycup gumweed gets its name from the sticky white resin that coats the tightly curled green bracts beneath each bright yellow bloom, and it flowers heavily from midsummer into fall when many other prairie natives have finished. That late, resinous bloom makes it an important late-season nectar source for a wide range of bees, including many specialist and long-tongued species, as well as small butterflies. It tolerates drought, poor soil, and roadside conditions extremely well, and often behaves as a short-lived perennial that reseeds itself into disturbed ground.

planting.note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days, then surface-sow in moist to wet soil in full to partial sun once temperatures warm.

directions: Sow into consistently moist to wet soil along pond edges, ditches, or low meadow spots, pressing seed onto the surface without covering since it needs light to germinate. This slender native wildflower is an entirely different, well-behaved species from the invasive Eurasian purple loosestrife it is sometimes confused with, staying in a modest clump rather than spreading into wetlands. From midsummer into fall it produces slim spikes of small magenta-pink flowers along winged stems that draw in bumblebees, small native bees, and skipper butterflies. It pairs well with other wetland natives such as blue flag iris and swamp milkweed in a rain garden setting.

planting.note: Fall-sow so seed cold-stratifies naturally over winter, or moist-cold stratify 60 days before spring sowing into well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in dry to medium, well-drained soil in open woodland or a lightly shaded meadow edge, conditions that mimic the oak woodlands and clearings where it grows wild. Unlike the fall-blooming Symphyotrichum asters, this compact species flowers earlier, from midsummer into early fall, with flat-topped clusters of small white ray flowers held above narrow, slightly rough leaves. The blooms attract a range of small bees, wasps, and butterflies, and the low, tidy habit makes it useful as a front-of-border native alternative to taller asters. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form a modest colony over time rather than seeding aggressively.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Surface-sow in early spring on bare, disturbed soil in full sun; seed needs light and cool temperatures to germinate.

directions: Scatter seed onto bare mineral soil in full sun and press in without covering, since it is adapted to colonize open, disturbed ground such as burned areas, clearings, and roadsides. Fireweed sends up tall spires of bright magenta-pink flowers from bottom to top over several weeks in mid- to late summer, and is one of the most valuable late-season nectar plants for bumblebees and honeybees across its wide northern range. It spreads by rhizome and readily self-seeds via wind-borne fluffy seed, so it is best given its own bed or a naturalized area rather than a tidy border. Give it room to roam; once established it forms dramatic drifts of color that keep blooming as many other perennials fade.

planting.note: Direct-sow into lean, gritty, well-drained soil after the soil warms; established plants tolerate poor, rocky ground.

directions: Sow into fast-draining, lean soil in full sun and avoid rich beds or heavy irrigation, which shorten this drought-adapted plant's life; it thrives on neglect in gravelly or sandy sites across the western Great Plains and Southwest. From late summer into fall it produces abundant yellow, aster-like daisies over finely divided, spine-tipped foliage, blooming at a time when many other nectar sources have dried up. The late flowers draw numerous native bees, honeybees, and migrating butterflies, making it a useful addition to a xeriscape or rock garden pollinator planting. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or subshrub, often reseeding to persist in the same general area.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed for several weeks, then direct-sow shallowly in spring; division of established rhizome clumps is an easier, faster route.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun or light shade, giving it room to spread by rhizome since it forms colonies over time. Small, bell-shaped white to greenish flower clusters appear in early to midsummer and are disproportionately attractive to pollinators for their size, drawing large numbers of native bees, honeybees, and butterflies, including many that get their tongues briefly trapped by the flower's sticky pollen mechanism. The milky latex sap and reddish stems distinguish it from true hemp, and the plant was historically used by Indigenous peoples for its strong bast fibers. Because it spreads assertively once established, it is best placed in a naturalized meadow or pollinator patch rather than a small formal bed.

planting.note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early spring, or cold-stratify and direct-sow seed shallowly once the soil has warmed.

directions: Site in well-drained soil in partial sun to light shade at a woodland edge or dry meadow margin, where its wiry, branching red-tinged stems and pairs of oval leaves form a low, spreading colony. Clusters of small, fragrant, pink-striped bell flowers nod from the branch tips in early summer and are intensely attractive to bumblebees, small butterflies, and moths, which are drawn to the sweet nectar despite the flower's slick, trap-like structure. The milky sap it shares with its dogbane relatives makes the foliage unpalatable to deer and rabbits, a useful trait in a naturalized pollinator planting. Give it space to spread underground and avoid rich, heavily amended soil, which encourages floppy growth.
